newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU parliament approves ferry, air accident laws.
newsitem.headline: EU parliament approves ferry, air accident laws.

text.p: The European Parliament on Wednesday approved new EU laws designed to reduce accidents at sea and increase insurance protection for aeroplane passengers.

Parliament said one of the laws -- a draft directive on compulsory registration of ferry passengers -- should be extended to cover cars using the Britain-France Channel Tunnel rail link which was badly damaged by a fire last November.
Euro-MPs pointed out that under current Tunnel registration procedures, fire brigades are unable to tell how many people might be trapped inside during an accident.

EU Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock told the EU assembly on Thursday it was not legally possible to extend the ferry bill to cover the tunnel but he promised to consider specific legislation for the Folkestone-Calais link.

The new ferry passenger law will bring all 15 countries in the EU bloc into line with a recent International Maritime Organisation (IMO) convention designed to make sailing safer by ensuring ferries do not exceed their maximum passenger capacity and making search and rescue operations easier.
The new rules come almost exactly 10 years after Britain's worst ferry disaster, when the Herald of Free Enterprise capsized on a voyage from England to Belgium.
The ferry sank in about three minutes killing 191 people.

Repeated calls for safety improvements, including an unheeded recommendation by the inquiry into the disaster for the compulsory use of watertight bulkheads, did not prevent a further tragedy in 1994 when another roll-on roll-off ferry, the Estonia, sank in the Baltic with the loss of over 900 lives.
Euro-MPs also gave a first reading to a draft directive which sets EU-wide minimum training standards for ship crews.

The new rules will bring EU regulations into line with a 1995 IMO convention on training and watch-keeping designed to limit human error, which parliament estimates is the cause of 80 percent of the 230 serious sea accidents which occur every year.
Euro-MPs said the same training standards should also apply to crews on third country vessels using EU ports.
Turning to air travel, the parliament gave a second reading to plans to increase airlines' liability for plane accidents.
At present, air carrier liability is limited by the 1929 Warsaw Convention to a maximum of $10,000.

The new regulation waives all financial limits of liability where the airline is at fault, allows passengers to claim compensation of up to 120,000 Ecus ($137,088) even if the carrier did all it could to avoid the accident and provides for advance hardship payments to victims.

Euro-deputies said they realised the EU could not impose the new rules on third country airlines operating in Europe but said that in the interests of fair competition, Brussels should seek commitments from outsiders to adopt similar levels of liabilty.
EU transport ministers are due to examine all three draft laws at a meeting in Luxembourg on June 17. All three need the support of parliament and ministers before they can become law.
